title: One URL and one key per agent
body: Every client gets its own key, its own view and its own revocation. Keys are compared in constant time and never reach a log line. altKeys lets you rotate one without cutting the agent off.

title: A key in the URL, for clients that cannot send headers
body: At least one widely used agent cannot send an Authorization header. Those clients get /k/<key>/mcp — and then the whole URL is a secret, so the gateway never writes a request path anywhere.

title: Profiles that filter the list and the call
body: A profile is the reusable half (what a kind of agent gets), the client is the specific half. Filtering applies to tools/list and is checked again on every call, so a hidden tool is not a callable one.

title: Exclusions accumulate, so deny always wins
body: Layers merge parents-first and the client last. Scalars are replaced by the most specific layer; exclusions only ever grow. A deny a later layer could undo is not a deny.

title: find_tool and call_tool, for clients that load everything
body: Some clients put every tool definition in every prompt. In search mode the gateway shows two tools and keeps the catalogue on the server, with its own BM25 index. Tools stay callable by name: an agent that remembers one should not be punished for it.

title: Rewrite a tool's wording without touching its server
body: Title, description and hints are yours to change; the input schema is not, because that is the server's contract. The research on tool descriptions says concrete beats long, and a server's own wording is often neither.

title: Response limits with an honest note
body: A single reply that fills the context window is worse than a trimmed one. Text is cut largest-first and the agent is told how much went and what to do instead.

title: The token bill, per source
body: jackfield tools --by-source prints how many tools each upstream contributes, how many KB of definitions, and roughly how many tokens that is. You cannot decide what to cut without seeing the bill.

title: Collisions resolved, never silently dropped
body: Prefix always, only on collision, or never. Names are capped at the 128 characters MCP allows; one that would overflow is trimmed with a hash rather than truncated into a duplicate. A tool that disappears quietly is worse than one with an odd name.

title: The whole gateway in one file you can review
body: No database, no admin panel writing state behind your back. Secrets are referenced with ${env:NAME} or ${file:/path}, resolved at startup, and registered for redaction so they cannot be printed. A deployment is a diff.

title: A restart your agents recover from by themselves
body: An unknown session id gets 404, which is the protocol's signal to start a new one. Answer 400 instead — as gateways do — and clients retry a dead session until a human reconnects them.

title: Long calls that stay alive
body: Upstream progress is forwarded on the originating call's own stream. Without that detail it lands on the standalone stream, which most clients never open, so the agent watches a long call sit silent and gives up.

title: One broken server does not take the rest with it
body: An unreachable upstream is left out of the catalogue and named in the gateway's instructions, so the agent is told what is missing instead of finding a hole. Set failOpen: false where a silent absence would be worse.

title: Listing opens nothing
body: Catalogues are shared per client and cached, so tools/list costs nothing once warm. Only a real call connects, and only to the upstream that owns the tool: two tools used does not mean twenty servers woken.

title: Find out when something sensitive runs
body: A line to ntfy or a webhook before and after any call you mark sensitive, and on every refusal. Fire-and-forget by design: a notifier that is down must never delay or fail a tool call.

title: Credentials held centrally, with OAuth upstream
body: Token files and headers work today. What is missing is an OAuth flow towards servers that require it, with refresh and encrypted storage, so no client ever holds a credential.

title: A read-only view of what each client sees
body: Planned as read-only on purpose: a panel that mutates state would move the real configuration somewhere you cannot read it in a diff.

title: Servers can talk back: forms, sampling, roots
body: MCP lets a server ask the agent for something mid-call — a login code, a confirmation, a completion. Jackfield bridges those requests to the agent that made the call, and when the agent cannot answer it says so instead of hanging. This is the half most gateways drop.

title: Allow, ask, or deny — per tool
body: ask puts the question to the user through an MCP form before the call runs. A client that cannot show forms is refused rather than waved through: an approval the agent grants itself is not an approval. Global rules are a floor; a client can tighten, never loosen.

title: Approve from outside the conversation
body: A link to a page of your own, with a passkey and a capture of what is about to happen, so the approval never lives inside the thing being approved. Needs a store of pending approvals; not started.

title: Child-process servers, wherever they can run
body: Any stdio MCP server, either in the gateway itself or on an executor. The same upstream definition works in both places, so moving one is a two-line edit and not a migration.

title: A core that cannot run processes, and a machine that can
body: A serverless function cannot keep a session, start a child process, or hold a stream open for an hour. Instead of letting the host decide what your tools may be, the executor runs on a machine you own and serves exactly those upstreams behind one token.

title: A command line as one tool, instead of a hundred
body: A service whose MCP server defines 120 tools, used twice a month, costs its definitions in every prompt. Its command line costs one. No shell ever — the program is spawned with an argument array — plus a fixed executable, an optional subcommand allow-list, denied arguments, a time limit and an output cap.

title: A terminal with permissions per command
body: Covered on the machine the executor runs on, by the same cli upstream: named commands, no shell, no free root. What is missing is reaching several machines from one executor.

title: A browser with saved sessions
body: Today a browser-automation server is just another HTTP upstream — and the form bridge is what makes it work through a gateway at all. Hosting one inside the executor, with stored sessions and your own egress address, is not started.

title: An executor that dials out, with no port to open
body: Today the core calls the executor, which listens on a private network. Reversing that — the executor opens the connection — would remove the last inbound port. Designed, not built.

title: A plain process
body: jackfield serve. The default, and the only one where everything works: sessions, forms, streams that stay open, child processes.

title: systemd, hardened
body: A unit file with no new privileges, a read-only system, a single read-only secrets directory, and a restricted set of address families.

title: Docker
body: A multi-stage image and a compose file with a health check. Mount secrets as files rather than passing them as environment variables.

title: NixOS, as a module
body: services.jackfield with options, plus the executor as a second unit. The configuration goes to the Nix store, which is world-readable, so every secret is a file reference and the module creates that directory at mode 0700.

title: Serverless, as one option among several
body: The HTTP layer is written against Web Request/Response, so a function is five lines of adapter. It needs stateless: true, and that costs sessions, forms and child processes — which is exactly what the executor is for. The platform specifics are written but not yet verified on a live deployment.

title: 53 tests, on the parts that matter
body: Aggregation, name collisions, profiles, search mode, overrides, trimming, permissions, notifications, forms, progress, sessions, stateless mode, the command-line sandbox, and a split core/executor setup end to end.

title: Code mode, sandboxed on the executor
body: Let the model write a short script that calls the tools and return only the result. The published numbers come from vendors, so this waits until there is a case that needs it.

title: Search by meaning, locally
body: BM25 is cheap and has no model to host. Local embeddings would catch paraphrases it misses.

title: More than one person
body: Separate people, not just separate agents, with no shared view and no shared keys.

title: A catalogue you install from
body: Known servers, added with one command — without the configuration ceasing to be a file you can read.
